name: Cryolipolysis (CoolSculpting Mini Chin)

card.summary: Fat freezing under the chin: a cleared non-surgical option with modest measured fat reduction and a rare paradoxical-growth side effect.
card.note: Reviews rate data quality as low; rare paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (enlargement of treated fat) has been reported.

quick.overview:
Cryolipolysis is a non-invasive procedure that uses controlled cold to reduce small pockets of fat. Under the chin (the submental area, often called a double chin) it is one of the treatment sites cleared by the US FDA, and a smaller applicator is sometimes marketed as a mini-chin treatment.

In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a non-surgical way to sharpen the jaw-neck line. Systematic reviews report modest average reductions in fat thickness, and the evidence base is described by reviewers as low in quality.
quick.mechanism: A device cools the skin and underlying subcutaneous fat over a set period. Cold is intended to damage fat tissue in the treated area, which the body then gradually clears. Reviews measure the result as skinfold or ultrasound fat-thickness change over following months.
quick.risks: Commonly reported effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, usually resolving within weeks. A rare effect, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which the treated fat enlarges, is reported at roughly 0.12% to 1.0% depending on the study, and surgical options such as liposuction are described for treating it.

lead: Cryolipolysis, commonly called fat freezing and sold under the CoolSculpting brand, is a non-invasive procedure that uses extreme cold applied to the skin to reduce subcutaneous fat in targeted areas [1]. The submental area under the chin is one of the sites for which the US FDA has cleared the technique, alongside the jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen and thighs [1].

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a non-surgical route to a more defined jaw-neck angle, sometimes under the label mini chin, referring to a smaller applicator used for the chin area. Systematic reviews of cryolipolysis in general report average fat-thickness reductions of a few millimeters and high patient satisfaction, while rating the quality of the data as low [1].
infobox: Submental area, jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen, thighs and others [1]

paras: The procedure applies controlled cooling to a fold of skin and fat for a set session. It is performed in a clinic without incisions or anesthesia, and is marketed to people with small, localized fat deposits rather than as a weight-loss method [1].

Zeltiq Aesthetics developed the technology and introduced it in the United States in 2010 under the CoolSculpting name. Allergan Aesthetics acquired Zeltiq in 2017, with the acquisition reported as completed on April 28, 2017 [1].

A 2015 systematic review of 19 studies reported average skinfold-thickness reductions between about 10% and 28.5%, with high satisfaction among patients [1]. A 2023 review of 18 studies reported average ultrasound-measured fat-thickness reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm and concluded the procedure appears safe and modestly effective, while rating the quality of the underlying data as low [1].
Commonly reported effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, which usually resolve within weeks [1].

Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which the treated fat grows instead of shrinking, is reported as rare, with published rates ranging from 0.12% to 1.0% depending on the study. Described treatments include liposuction or abdominoplasty [1].

Reviews of cryolipolysis across body areas are summarized above [1]. A small trial of fat reduction in the submandibular and submental area (14 participants, started February 2016) is registered as completed on ClinicalTrials.gov; no results are given in the registration record available here [2].

timeline.event: Zeltiq introduces CoolSculpting in the United States [1]
Allergan Aesthetics completes acquisition of Zeltiq [1]
Registered submandibular/submental fat reduction trial begins (n=14) [2]
